metadata.title: Pattern Recognition: Feature Selection KP06 Feature Subset Selection
metadata.description: Pattern Recognition, Feature Selection unit, KP06 feature subset selection; guided v1; English self-study; answer first then feedback

scene-root.name: Pattern Recognition: Feature Selection KP06 Feature Subset Selection

scene-u01.name: Pattern Recognition: Feature Selection KP06 Feature Subset Selection

p01-rank-title.name: p01-rank-title
p01-rank-title.text: Are the three features with the highest individual scores the best three?

p01-rank-ctx.name: p01-rank-ctx
p01-rank-ctx.text: 5 features, 100 samples per class (teaching setup, seed 0): compute one $|t|$ per feature (KP03) and sort from large to small.

p01-rank-tp.name: p01-rank-tp
p01-rank-tp.text: By individual score only: the top three are $\{x_1,\ x_2,\ x_3\}$ (gold background)

p01-rank-wn.name: p01-rank-wn
p01-rank-wn.text: $x_1$ and $x_2$ are correlated $0.99$ (redundant); $x_5$ has the smallest $|t|$ alone and looks completely useless...

p02-step2-title.name: p02-step2-title
p02-step2-title.text: Remedy 1: when choosing the second feature, subtract how much it resembles the chosen one

p02-step2-ctx.name: p02-step2-ctx
p02-step2-ctx.text: $x_1$ is chosen. Candidate score $=C(j)-0.4\,|\rho_{1j}|$ ($C$ = individual score, $\rho$ = correlation with $x_1$).

p02-step2-pk.name: p02-step2-pk
p02-step2-pk.text: The second pick is not $x_2$, second by individual score, but $x_3$ ($0.76$)

p03-step3-title.name: p03-step3-title
p03-step3-title.text: Third step: compare similarity with the average of all chosen ones

p03-step3-ctx.name: p03-step3-ctx
p03-step3-ctx.text: $x_1$ and $x_3$ are chosen. Each candidate subtracts its average correlation with both: $C(j)-0.4\times\overline{|\rho|}$.

p03-step3-sel.name: p03-step3-sel
p03-step3-sel.text: $x_1$ and $x_3$ chosen; the correlation $0.95$ of $x_2$ with $x_1$ is still very high

p03-step3-lim.name: p03-step3-lim
p03-step3-lim.text: The result $\{x_1,x_3,x_4\}$ differs from the individual top three $\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}$; but this is still picking step by step, does not compare whole sets and cannot see complementarity

p04-fw-title.name: p04-fw-title
p04-fw-title.text: Score the whole set: filter and wrapper have different flows

p04-fw-ctx.name: p04-fw-ctx
p04-fw-ctx.text: What is scored is a whole set of features. The difference: does the score come from a separability criterion, or from the classifier itself?

p04-fw-ft.name: p04-fw-ft
p04-fw-ft.text: Filter: scoring is independent of the classifier

p04-fw-wt.name: p04-fw-wt
p04-fw-wt.text: Wrapper: the classifier itself gives the score

p04-fw-w2.name: p04-fw-w2
p04-fw-w2.text:
Train the classifier
Compute validation error

p04-fw-w3.name: p04-fw-w3
p04-fw-w3.text: The set with the lowest error

p04-fw-bk.name: p04-fw-bk
p04-fw-bk.text: Finish one set, then try the next

p04-fw-cfn.name: p04-fw-cfn
p04-fw-cfn.text: Scoring $N$ sets is fast and the classifier is trained once: fast and clean; but a good criterion does not mean good final performance

p04-fw-cwn.name: p04-fw-cwn
p04-fw-cwn.text: Each cell = a complete training and validation of one subset: close to the real task, but far more costly

p05-combos-title.name: p05-combos-title
p05-combos-title.text: Combinatorial explosion: when scoring whole sets we cannot try every set

p05-combos-c3.name: p05-combos-c3
p05-combos-c3.text:
A wrapper trains the classifier once for every set
⇒ impossible to try one by one; and often $l$ is not even known in advance

p05-combos-rt.name: p05-combos-rt
p05-combos-rt.text:
Gap of $9.05$ ticks
(each tick $\times10$)
⇒ about $1.1\times10^{9}$ times
(a billion times)

p05-combos-nt.name: p05-combos-nt
p05-combos-nt.text: On an equal-proportion scale: the right bar would be half a wall high and the left bar less than 1 pixel

p06-comp-title.name: p06-comp-title
p06-comp-title.text: Complementarity: $x_5$ is useless alone, yet cancels the noise of $x_4$

p06-comp-ctx.name: p06-comp-ctx
p06-comp-ctx.text: $x_4$ = class signal + large noise; $x_5$ = only the same noise. Drawn in the $(x_4,\ x_5)$ plane.

p06-comp-xa.name: p06-comp-xa
p06-comp-xa.text: The two classes line up along a slanted band and separate only in the direction perpendicular to the band

p06-comp-a4.name: p06-comp-a4
p06-comp-a4.text:
$x_4$ only: accuracy on new data $0.60$
(the noise is too large, almost inseparable)

p06-comp-a5.name: p06-comp-a5
p06-comp-a5.text:
$x_5$ only: accuracy $0.49$
(guessing level, looks completely useless)

p06-comp-ab.name: p06-comp-ab
p06-comp-ab.text:
$x_4$ and $x_5$ together: $0.87$
$x_4-x_5\approx$ class signal (the noise is subtracted)

p06-comp-ls.name: p06-comp-ls
p06-comp-ls.text: Individual scoring threw away this key partner and kept both redundant $x_1$ and $x_2$

p07-sim-title.name: p07-sim-title
p07-sim-title.text: Filter versus wrapper measured: individual top three vs the three chosen by validation

p07-sim-ctx.name: p07-sim-ctx
p07-sim-ctx.text: Blue bar = 5-fold validation accuracy on the training data; gold bar = accuracy on 4000 new samples (vertical axis starts at 0.5).

p07-sim-cc.name: p07-sim-cc
p07-sim-cc.text: The wrapper result with three features is almost as good as with all 5 features

p08-val-title.name: p08-val-title
p08-val-title.text: How many features to keep: read the validation error, not the training error

p08-val-ctx.name: p08-val-ctx
p08-val-ctx.text: Only 20 training samples per class; the signal of feature $i$ is $1/\sqrt i$ (weaker for later ones); repeated 40 times and averaged.

p08-val-lg0.name: p08-val-lg0
p08-val-lg0.text: Training error: falls all the way to 0.001

p08-val-lg1.name: p08-val-lg1
p08-val-lg1.text: Validation error: first falls, then rises

p08-val-lg2.name: p08-val-lg2
p08-val-lg2.text: New-data error: first falls, then rises

p08-val-mc.name: p08-val-mc
p08-val-mc.text:
Validation error is lowest at $l=50$ ($0.037$)
New-data error is lowest at $l=80$

p08-val-ct.name: p08-val-ct
p08-val-ct.text: The training error gives no hint of where to stop; the lowest point of the validation error is close to the lowest point on new data

p09-bias-title.name: p09-bias-title
p09-bias-title.text: Selecting features is itself learning: selecting on all data then validating makes the score too high

p09-bias-ctx.name: p09-bias-ctx
p09-bias-ctx.text: The data is pure noise: 1000 features and 40 samples (20 per class); the true accuracy can only be $0.5$. Repeated 20 times.

p09-bias-bn0.name: p09-bias-bn0
p09-bias-bn0.text:
Select 10 on all the data first,
then cross-validate

p09-bias-bn1.name: p09-bias-bn1
p09-bias-bn1.text:
Selection inside each fold
(training data of the fold only)

p09-bias-ct.name: p09-bias-ct
p09-bias-ct.text: On the same noise data: select-then-validate gets $0.88$; put the selection inside each fold and it returns to the guessing $0.49$

p09-bias-rs.name: p09-bias-rs
p09-bias-rs.text: Reason: feature selection used samples that later serve as validation, so information leaks (the same kind as the data leakage of KP02)

p10-pipe-title.name: p10-pipe-title
p10-pipe-title.text: The right flow: feature selection happens inside the training data of each fold

p10-pipe-ctx.name: p10-pipe-ctx
p10-pipe-ctx.text: Both are 5-fold cross-validation; the two flows differ in where "select features" is placed; the bars on the right are the accuracies the two flows give.

p10-pipe-w1.name: p10-pipe-w1
p10-pipe-w1.text: Select the 10 features with the largest $|t|$ using all the data

p10-pipe-w2.name: p10-pipe-w2
p10-pipe-w2.text:
Split into 5 folds and cross-validate
(the validation data has already been seen)

p10-pipe-r1.name: p10-pipe-r1
p10-pipe-r1.text: Each fold: select features and train using the training part only

p10-pipe-r2.name: p10-pipe-r2
p10-pipe-r2.text:
Evaluate on the validation part of the fold
(the validation data has not been seen)

p10-pipe-cd.name: p10-pipe-cd
p10-pipe-cd.text:
scikit-learn: make_pipeline(SelectKBest(f_classif, k=10), LinearDiscriminantAnalysis())
then cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=5): every fold re-selects the features

p11-practice1-title.name: p11-practice1-title
p11-practice1-title.text: Exercise 1: choosing 4 from 30 features, how many combinations?

p11-practice1-ctx.name: p11-practice1-ctx
p11-practice1-ctx.text: Work it out yourself first, then press Next for feedback.

p11-practice1-q1.name: p11-practice1-q1
p11-practice1-q1.text: Exercise 1: choosing $l=4$ from $m=30$ features, how many combinations in all?

p11-practice1-pool.name: p11-practice1-pool
p11-practice1-pool.text: Candidate pool: 30 features (each dot is a feature)

p11-practice1-blb.name: p11-practice1-blb
p11-practice1-blb.text: All 657,720 "ordered" selections drawn as one long bar; every $4!=24$ cells are the 24 orderings of the same set of features

p11-practice1-ans.name: p11-practice1-ans
p11-practice1-ans.text:
Every $4!=24$ cells are the same set of features reordered
⇒ 657,720 ÷ 24 = 27,405 combinations

p11-practice1-cm.name: p11-practice1-cm
p11-practice1-cm.text: Only 30 features and choosing just 4 already gives over twenty-seven thousand sets; with a little larger $m$, $l$ enumeration is impossible

p12-practice2-title.name: p12-practice2-title
p12-practice2-title.text: Exercise 2: pick the second feature with the correlation correction

p12-practice2-ctx.name: p12-practice2-ctx
p12-practice2-ctx.text: Work it out yourself first, then press Next for feedback.

p12-practice2-q2.name: p12-practice2-q2
p12-practice2-q2.text: Exercise 2: three features have individual scores $C=0.95,\ 0.90,\ 0.60$. $x_1$ is chosen, $|\rho_{12}|=0.97$, $|\rho_{13}|=0.10$, with $\alpha_1=1$ and $\alpha_2=0.5$. Whom do you pick second?

p12-practice2-pk.name: p12-practice2-pk
p12-practice2-pk.text: Pick $x_3$ second: although its individual score is only $0.60$, it is hardly similar to $x_1$

p13-summary-title.name: p13-summary-title
p13-summary-title.text: The whole KP06: pick a set, not the highest scores one by one

p13-summary-ctx.name: p13-summary-ctx
p13-summary-ctx.text: One chart closes the unit: the bars are the accuracies of the various methods and the dashed line is guessing; the three blocks are the three steps of this KP in order.

p13-summary-src1.name: p13-summary-src1
p13-summary-src1.text: Simulated data (seed 0): accuracy on 4000 new samples

p13-summary-src2.name: p13-summary-src2
p13-summary-src2.text: Pure noise data: mean of cross-validation repeated 20 times

p13-summary-cA.name: p13-summary-cA
p13-summary-cA.text:
Individual top three only $0.75$
(redundant, misses complementarity)

p13-summary-cB.name: p13-summary-cB
p13-summary-cB.text:
Scoring whole sets: three features $0.89$ ≈ all five $0.90$
$\binom{100}{10}\approx1.7\times10^{13}$ sets cannot be enumerated; read $l$ from the validation error

p13-summary-cC1.name: p13-summary-cC1
p13-summary-cC1.text:
Select first, validate later
inflated to $0.88$

p13-summary-cC2.name: p13-summary-cC2
p13-summary-cC2.text:
Put inside each fold
back to $0.49$ (inflated by $0.39$)

p13-summary-next.name: p13-summary-next
p13-summary-next.text: The next KP asks: with too many subsets to enumerate, how do we walk cleverly step by step? ⇒ Forward, backward and floating search

steps.label: Pattern Recognition: Feature Selection KP06 Feature Subset Selection
Are the three features with the highest individual scores the best three? · Look at the axes and the 5 features first: one score per feature.
